prompt: In a Selenium test against Chrome, which program actually works the browser?

choices.text: `chromedriver`, which the test sends HTTP requests to
choices.why: Right. The test is an HTTP client, the driver an HTTP server, and only the driver touches Chrome.

choices.text: Selenium code injected into the page, the way a browser extension adds its own
choices.why: Nothing of Selenium runs inside the page; that picture belongs to tools like Cypress, lesson 9.

choices.text: The test process, through a browser extension it installs into Chrome first
choices.why: No extension is involved: the test only speaks HTTP to a driver.

choices.text: Node's test runner
choices.why: `node:test` only runs the test functions; it knows nothing about browsers.

prompt: Put the requests of the session you held by hand with `curl` in order.
trap: Every address after the first carries the session id, so nothing can come before `POST /session`.

prompt: `POST /session/{id}/element` answered `{"value":{"element-6066-11e4-a52e-4f735466cecf":"f.A30D…e.3"}}`. What did you get back?

choices.text: The element's HTML
choices.why: No markup came back; to learn its text you had to send a second request.

choices.text: A reference the driver uses to name that node
choices.why: Right. Anything about the element is a further request carrying that reference.

choices.text: An error code, because the key looks like a fault number
choices.why: That odd key is fixed by the standard so no page's own JSON can be mistaken for an element.

choices.text: The heading's text, encoded so that it travels safely inside JSON
choices.why: The text came from `GET .../text`, as `{"value":"Banana"}`.

prompt: A test finds the basket count, then the page redraws the whole header, then the test reads the element it found. What does the protocol predict?

choices.text: The new count, since the reference follows the selector
choices.why: A reference names a node, not a selector; it is not looked up again.

choices.text: An error: the reference names a node that is gone
choices.why: Right. The reference has gone stale, and the driver says so.

choices.text: The old count, cached by the driver
choices.why: The driver keeps no copy of the text; every read is a new request to the page.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since a test pauses the page between commands
choices.why: The page goes on running between requests; that is why it can change under the test.

prompt: The Selenium test fails at once because nothing answers on port 3000. Which step did the student skip?

choices.text: Running `npx playwright install chromium`
choices.why: That fetches Playwright's browser; it starts no server.

choices.text: Adding a `webServer` block to `selenium/shop.test.js`, as in Playwright's config
choices.why: `webServer` is a Playwright configuration option; `node:test` has nothing like it.

choices.text: Starting the shop with `npm start` in another terminal
choices.why: Right. With Selenium and `node:test`, nothing starts the shop for you.

choices.text: Calling `quit()` in `after`
choices.why: `quit()` closes the browser at the end; it has nothing to do with the shop being up.

prompt: Why does the test wait for the count to say `1` instead of reading it straight after `click()`?

choices.text: Selenium cannot read text from a header
choices.why: It reads any element's text; the issue is when, not where.

choices.text: `click()` returns once the click is dispatched, before the shop has necessarily answered
choices.why: Right. The count changes only when the shop's answer arrives, so the test waits for it.

choices.text: The count is only drawn once the toast has gone
choices.why: The script redraws the count first and then shows the toast.

choices.text: `assert.equal` cannot compare strings
choices.why: It compares strings fine; the final assert does exactly that.

prompt: Match each job to what does it in the Selenium test with `node:test`.
The wait timed out with `Waiting until element text is` and nothing more. What would make the next such failure say what went wrong?

choices.text: A longer timeout, so the message has time to fill in
choices.why: The message's wording does not depend on the timeout; only the wait's length changes.

choices.text: A message as `driver.wait`'s third argument
choices.why: Right. `driver.wait(condition, 5000, 'basket count never became 1')` puts your words in the error.

choices.text: An implicit wait set as well
choices.why: Mixing the two makes timing harder to predict and adds nothing to the message.

choices.text: The TAP reporter instead of `spec`
choices.why: Both reporters print the same error; TAP is only terser around it.

prompt: Match each browser to its driver.
The morning after Chrome updated itself to 141, every test fails with `This version of ChromeDriver only supports Chrome version 139`. What is the fix?

choices.text: Pin Chrome back to 139 in the test
choices.why: The test does not choose the browser's version; the installed Chrome is what it is.

choices.text: Retry the tests until one passes
choices.why: The driver refuses every session; no retry gets past a version check.

choices.text: A driver whose major version is 141; delete the old one on the `PATH`
choices.why: Right. Selenium Manager uses a driver it finds on the `PATH` first; remove the stale one and it fetches the right one.

choices.text: Change `forBrowser('chrome')` to `forBrowser('chromium')`, so that Selenium asks for a newer driver
choices.why: The browser is the same; the driver is still the one that does not match.

prompt: Driver 140 opened Chrome 141 and logged `has not been tested with Chrome version 141`. A colleague wants to leave it, since the tests pass. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: Leave it: a warning is not a failure
choices.why: Passing today is the driver guessing; the vendor's rule is the same major version.

choices.text: Replace it with a 141 driver, matching the browser's first number
choices.why: Right. Two versions behind and one ahead both refused outright; one behind only happens to work.

choices.text: Downgrade Chrome to 140 so the warning disappears
choices.why: Browsers update themselves; the driver is the part you keep in step.

choices.text: Switch to geckodriver, which accepts any Chrome
choices.why: geckodriver drives Firefox, not Chrome.

prompt: Where does Selenium Manager look for a driver before it downloads one?

choices.text: In `node_modules`
choices.why: Only Selenium Manager itself is in `node_modules`; drivers are not shipped there.

choices.text: On the `PATH`
choices.why: Right. Its log says `Found chromedriver ... in PATH`, and a stale one there wins.

choices.text: Inside Chrome's own installation folder
choices.why: Chrome does not ship its driver; the driver comes from Chrome for Testing.

choices.text: On the Selenium Grid at port 4444, if there is one running
choices.why: Selenium Manager knows nothing of a grid; a grid's node runs its own lookup.

prompt: With an implicit wait of 3000 ms, a test checks that no `.error` element exists. On a page with no error, how long does that check take?

choices.text: A few milliseconds, as finding the cards did
choices.why: That is what finding the cards took, because they existed; an absent element is the opposite case.

choices.text: The full three seconds, every time
choices.why: Right. It measured 3036 ms: an implicit wait cannot tell not yet from never.

choices.text: It never returns
choices.why: It returns an empty list when the timeout runs out.

choices.text: Half the timeout on average, since it stops looking at a random point
choices.why: There is no averaging: it keeps looking until the whole timeout is spent.

prompt: A test must wait for the toast to empty after it said `Added Banana`. Which wait can express that?

choices.text: An implicit wait, since the toast is an element that has been on the page all along
choices.why: An implicit wait only waits for an element to exist, and the toast always exists.

choices.text: Either kind, set to two seconds
choices.why: The length is not the problem; an implicit wait has no condition about text at all.

choices.text: An explicit wait on `until.elementTextIs(toast, '')`
choices.why: Right. It took 2115 ms in the capture, about the two seconds the script waits.

choices.text: None: a fixed sleep is the only way
choices.why: An explicit wait does it and returns as soon as it holds; lesson 13 is about why sleeping is worse.

prompt: What is the implicit timeout of a new session, in milliseconds, as the `timeouts` of the session you opened by hand showed?
What changes in a test to run it on a Selenium Grid instead of a local driver?

choices.text: Every command becomes a grid call
choices.why: The grid speaks the same WebDriver protocol, so the commands are the same.

choices.text: The address the builder sends requests to
choices.why: Right. `usingServer('http://localhost:4444')`, or `SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL`, and nothing else.

choices.text: The test runner, which must be Selenium's
choices.why: Selenium has no runner of its own; `node:test` ran the grid test unchanged.

choices.text: The selectors, which the router rewrites
choices.why: The router forwards requests; it does not touch what they ask for.

prompt: Which part of the grid decides which node a new session goes to?

choices.text: The router, since every request passes through it first
choices.why: The router is the address and forwards requests; the choice is made after the queue.

choices.text: The session map, which keeps track of every node it has
choices.why: It remembers which node holds a session once one exists; it does not choose.

choices.text: The distributor, matching capabilities to free slots
choices.why: Right. The log says `Session request received by the Distributor`, then the node creates it.

choices.text: The test, by naming one node's own address in `usingServer`
choices.why: The test only names the grid; it never learns which machine it got.

prompt: A single process holding the router, queue, distributor, session map and one node is started with `java -jar selenium-server-4.51.0.jar ___` .
A grid node runs on another machine. The test does `driver.get('http://localhost:3000/')` and the browser shows a connection error, though the shop runs on the tester's laptop. Why?

choices.text: The grid blocks port 3000 for every browser it hands out
choices.why: The grid has no say over which addresses a browser opens.

choices.text: The node's chromedriver is the wrong version for its Chrome
choices.why: A version mismatch refuses the session; here the session opened and the page failed.

choices.text: That address means the node's own computer, where nothing listens
choices.why: Right. On the node's machine nothing listens on 3000; the app needs an address the nodes can reach.

choices.text: `SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL` overrides the shop's address too
choices.why: It only says where the WebDriver requests go, not what the browser loads.

prompt: Selenium and Playwright both open the shop headless here. Which part of that was written into the Selenium test by hand?

choices.text: Nothing: both are headless by default
choices.why: Only Playwright is; Selenium opens a window unless told otherwise.

choices.text: The `--headless=new` argument in the Chrome options
choices.why: Right. It is Chrome's own switch, passed through Selenium; delete it to watch the run.

choices.text: A `headless: true` line in a configuration file
choices.why: The Selenium test has no configuration file; the option is in the code.

choices.text: An environment variable set before `node --test`
choices.why: The only variable in the lesson is `SELENIUM_REMOTE_URL`, which picks a server, not a mode.
